title: Anansi and Nothing
source: Barker & Sinclair, West African Folk-Tales (1917), tale III
lesson: Envy digs pits that only bring grief.
lines: Why do people say a crying child is crying for nothing? Blame Anansi. His neighbour was a rich man called Nothing.
Together they set off to find wives. Nothing wore fine velvet. Anansi wore ragged cotton. Let's swap clothes for a while, said Anansi.
He kept forgetting to swap back. Not yet, the road is dusty. Not yet, the sun is too hot.
Anansi, in velvet, found many wives. Ragged Nothing was laughed at, until a kind mother gave him her daughter.
But at the crossroads, Nothing's road led to a palace. Anansi's led to a hut. And Anansi's wives all moved to Nothing's palace.
Anansi was furious. He set a slippery trap at Nothing's door. Nothing fell, and did not get up again.
His widow gave every child she met some mashed yam, to help her cry. And children still cry for Nothing. Envy digs pits that only bring grief.
Next time: Anansi and the magic pot. Follow so you don't miss it!
